claims.text: SLM followed by solution annealing at 1400°C and aging at 1100°C will produce a BCC-dominated Nb-Mo-Ta-W-Zr microstructure.
The proposed processing route will generate a high density of coherent nanoscale B2-ordered precipitates.
The B2 precipitates will be Nb-rich or Ta-rich.
Rapid solidification and dynamic recrystallization during annealing will refine the grain size to below 5 µm.
Rapid solidification during SLM traps interstitial impurities within the lattice.
Lattice trapping of interstitial impurities prevents their segregation to grain boundaries.
Solution annealing at 1400°C dissolves brittle topologically close-packed phases.
Solution annealing at 1400°C homogenizes the alloy composition.
Aging at 1100°C for 30 minutes precipitates coherent B2 phases.
The coherent B2 precipitates impede dislocation motion through Orowan strengthening.
The short aging treatment avoids formation of large, brittle intermetallic phases.
Refined grains and coherent precipitates collectively enhance alloy strength.
Suppressing grain-boundary interstitial segregation mitigates brittleness.
The processed alloy will have a yield strength above 800 MPa at 1000°C.
The processed alloy will have room-temperature elongation to failure above 10%.
The processed alloy will significantly outperform conventionally cast or slowly cooled counterparts.
Conventionally cast or slowly cooled Nb-Mo-Ta-W-Zr alloys typically form brittle Laves or sigma phases.
Conventionally cast or slowly cooled Nb-Mo-Ta-W-Zr alloys typically exhibit less than 2% room-temperature ductility because of interstitial segregation and coarse microstructures.
Interstitial contents above 1000 ppm overwhelm the proposed trapping mechanisms.
Significant additions of Group III or Group VI elements can produce different phase stability and place the alloy outside the hypothesis boundary.

contradictions.description: The microstructure is described as single-phase BCC while also containing B2 precipitates as a distinct ordered phase; this is internally inconsistent unless 'single-phase' is intended to describe only the matrix.

The Nb-Mo-Ta-W-Zr family is characterized as consisting specifically of Group IV-V transition metals, but Mo and W are Group VI elements. The boundary also warns that significant Group VI additions may invalidate the hypothesis even though two Group VI elements are core constituents.
